sweep_summary: Capanahua is in the catalog as weight-sensitive (QS-FIXED: stress on the second syllable if closed by a non-glottal consonant, else initial; Loos 1969 ch. VII, read from page images by the qs-tier). Three title items: (1) Elias-Ulloa 2006 dissertation, already on file, read: confirms the primary rule with fieldwork-backed disyllabic footing, and refines the weight class — long-vowel second syllables also take the head ((ka.ˈpiː) 'crocodile', (ra.ˈbiː).bi 'both', p.173), while closed odd syllables are light (p.179); secondary feet iterate. (2) Safir 1979 (MITWPL 1:95-114): no open copy found anywhere; per Hagberg 1993 it re-analyses Loos's data and is the source of the iterative secondary-stress coding; priority medium. (3) Hagberg 1993/2006 dissertation: fetched sources from archive.org (new file), sec. 4.2 pp.212-215 gives a second-hand summary of Loos 1969 ('Stress occurs on the second syllable if it is closed (i.e., heavy), otherwise it falls on the first syllable'; monosyllables unstressed) — confirms. Two further on-disk sources read: Elias-Ulloa 2021 (Languages 6:158, first-hand, explicit two-syllable-window statement — the best new statement; confirms) and González 2017 (Amerindia 39, secondary survey; refines: heavy = coda, long vowel or nasalized vowel). Nothing supersedes Loos 1969 as the deciding source, but the catalog's 'no vowel-length criterion' should be annotated: Elias-Ulloa's data show CVː second syllables attracting stress.

new_statements.reading: A first-hand fieldworker's explicit statement: weight-sensitive stress in a two-syllable left window, peninitial iff the second syllable is closed, else initial, with high pitch on the stressed syllable. It matches the catalog's QS-FIXED 'peninitial if heavy else initial' coding from Loos 1969 exactly. Elias-Ulloa 2006 p.173 (also read, page image) adds that a long second-syllable vowel likewise takes the head ((ka.ˈpiː) 'crocodile', (ra.ˈbiː).bi 'both'), so 'heavy' should be read as CVC-or-CVː rather than the catalog's 'no vowel-length criterion' (which is faithful to Loos 1969 alone), and p.179 states that closed odd syllables are light (a closed initial syllable never draws stress off an initial default).

audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Loos 1969 page images at book pp.190-191 (PDF pp.204-205), and the supporting p.193/p.194 passages are where the locator says. (2) The classification rests on the primary phonology monograph for the language (Loos 1969, ch. VII), not a second-hand or pedagogical source. Three later works fetched sources now -- Elias-Ulloa 2006 (Rutgers PhD, own fieldwork), González 2017 (Amerindia Panoan metrical typology) and Elias-Ulloa 2021 (Languages) -- all state the same primary-stress rule: two-syllable initial window, stress on σ2 if closed (Elias-Ulloa 2006/González add: or long/nasalized vowel), else σ1, stressed syllable high-pitched. So kind=weight, edge=left, non-glottal CVC heavy is confirmed. sources.note: First-hand (author's fieldwork): two-syllable left window; main stress peninitial iff the second syllable is closed, else initial; stressed syllable carries high pitch; closed first syllables do not attract stress ([ˈmis.kʊ], [ˈmɨs.kʊ.ti]); Capanahua allows glottal-stop codas and [ˈtɨʔ.wɨ.ti] 'to limp' has initial stress. Stress shifts when suffixation closes the second syllable.

sources.quote: El shipibo y el capanahua tienen sistemas acentuales muy similares ... En ambos, el acento principal se asigna por lo general en la primera sílaba de la palabra, (20a, b; 21a, b) excepto si la segunda sílaba tiene coda, vocal larga o nasalizada (20c-f; 21c-e) (Loos 1969: 191, 192; Valenzuela 2003: 107-108; Elías-Ulloa 2004: 3, 2006: 17-21; este volumen). Las consonantes que pueden ser codas en shipibo y capanahua son /n, s, ʃ, ʂ/ (Valenzuela 2003: 98; Loos 1969). (21) Acento principal en capanahua (Elías-Ulloa 2006: 173) a. [ˈbɨʃ.pi] 'brote de planta' b. [ˈʔi.ku.nin] 'sobrino' c. [ka.ˈpɨː] 'caimán' d. [ra.ˈbɨː.bi] 'los dos' e. [kɨʂ.ˈkan.kin] 'inclinarse' [Translation: Shipibo and Capanahua have very similar stress systems ... In both, main stress is generally assigned to the first syllable of the word, except if the second syllable has a coda, a long vowel or a nasalized vowel.]

sources.note: Secondary survey (built on Loos 1969 and Elías-Ulloa 2006): main stress initial unless the second syllable is heavy, where heavy = coda consonant, long vowel or nasalized vowel; classed as 'non-cohesive, initial' (type 5.1), i.e. quantity-sensitive with a left-edge default; Elías-Ulloa's disyllabic-foot analysis with iterative secondary feet is reported. fn.24 notes exceptions (about 1% of the lexicon with stress on an open second syllable, loans, monosyllabic roots with stress-attracting clitics) that Elías-Ulloa reports for Shipibo in the same volume.

sources.quote: Another language in which Weight-to-Stress apparently applies only to a foot-bound heavy syllable is Capanahua, a language of Peru. The following is a summary of the relevant facts, taken from Loos 1969; the same data are found in Safir 1979. According to Loos 1969, Capanahua has both stress and high tone. These have distinct but predictable distributions which differ as follows. Stress occurs on the second syllable if it is closed (i.e., heavy), otherwise it falls on the first syllable. High tone, like stress, occurs on the second syllable if it is closed but, unlike stress, it falls on each of the first two syllables if the second syllable is not closed. [p.212] ... Monosyllables lack stress and high tone [p.212]
sources.locator: sec. 4.2, diss. pp. 212-215 (PDF pp. 216-219); Capanahua summary p.212, data (11)-(12) pp.212-213, analysis (13)-(15) pp.213-215, fn. 10 p.214
sources.note: Second-hand (from Loos 1969 and Safir 1979): one stress per word, on the second syllable if closed, else on the first; monosyllables (clitics ta?, ra?, ris and pronouns ?in, min, han) unstressed and toneless; high tone on the stressed syllable spreading rightward within the foot. Analysis: syllabic feet built iteratively L-to-R (evidence = every-other-syllable glottal deletion, following Safir 1979), Weight-to-Stress applies once per word within the first foot (heavy = consonant-final). fn.10: words with both first and second syllables heavy untested in Loos's data.
